common_name: UConn Wedding Bells Carolina Silverbell (Compact Large-Flowered Silverbell)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; UConn Wedding Bells is a compact, rounded Carolina silverbell selection well suited to smaller residential lots where the straight species would eventually outgrow the space.

directions: Selected and introduced by breeder Mark Brand at the University of Connecticut, UConn Wedding Bells is a smaller, denser, more rounded form of Carolina silverbell than typical seedling trees, topping out around 20 feet rather than the 30-plus feet of the species. Its white, dangling, bell-shaped flowers in early May are noticeably larger than those of the species and flare open more fully, giving a showier, more visible display along the branches, and the glossy foliage has a slightly more refined texture. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, siting it where its shrubby, multi-trunked silhouette and clean yellow fall color can be appreciated up close rather than as a distant canopy tree. Like other silverbells it establishes slowly and resents root disturbance, so choose a permanent site for young container-grown stock.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, which can scorch the variegated leaf margins; site as an understory specimen beneath taller canopy trees.

directions: Variegata is a rare sport of mountain silverbell prized for foliage edged in an irregular, creamy-yellow margin unlike the variegation pattern of almost any other woody plant, brightening the deep partial shade where mountain silverbell is typically sited. It still carries the species' spectacular April display of nodding, pure-white, bell-shaped flowers dangling in rows beneath the branches before the leaves fully expand, followed by four-winged seed pods that persist into winter. Because variegated foliage is more prone to leaf scorch than the solid green species, give it a site with dappled or morning sun and afternoon shade rather than the full sun some silverbells will tolerate, and keep soil consistently moist and acidic. Grows slowly compared to green-leaved seedlings, so allow extra years for it to reach a substantial size.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Snowcone is a uniform, nursery-selected Japanese snowbell bred for predictable pyramidal form and reliable cold hardiness.

directions: Introduced by J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. in 2002 as selection 'JFS-D', Snowcone was chosen from seedling populations for its dense, uniform, broadly pyramidal habit and consistent performance, addressing the variability and winter tip dieback common in seed-grown Japanese snowbell. It produces the same profuse clusters of pendulous, mildly fragrant white bells in June as the species, set against refined dark-green foliage that turns yellow to red-toned in fall, and it flowers heavily even on relatively young trees. Later bud break than typical seedling stock helps it dodge damage from late spring frosts in colder parts of its range. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade in hotter regions, and expect a far more predictable mature shape than trees grown from open-pollinated seed.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Chinese snowbell is still scarce in North American gardens but performs like its better-known relatives, needing consistent moisture and protection from harsh afternoon sun.

directions: Styrax confusus is an attractive, tree-forming snowbell from central and southern China, valued for larger leaves than the familiar Styrax japonicus and showy racemes carrying several white, bell-shaped flowers together in early summer rather than the single dangling flowers typical of many snowbells. It remains uncommon in cultivation but has proven garden-worthy in specialty collections and arboreta, forming a small, rounded tree with the same refined, horizontal branching that makes the genus prized for underplanting taller shade trees. Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, mimicking the woodland-margin conditions of its native range, and shelter young plants from drying wind while they establish. Like other snowbells it resents root disturbance once planted, so choose a permanent site for container-grown stock.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in light, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light shade; storax is native to rocky Mediterranean and Middle Eastern slopes and dislikes wet, poorly drained ground, especially in winter.

directions: Native to rocky slopes, open woods, and thickets from the eastern Mediterranean to the Middle East, storax is a large deciduous shrub or small tree bearing fragrant, bell-shaped white flowers in axillary clusters from May into June, followed by small gray-felted fruits historically harvested as a source of resin and incense. It is naturally adapted to lean, fast-draining, sandy or loamy soils and full sun, though it tolerates light or dappled shade, especially where summers run hot and dry. Once established it is notably drought-tolerant and needs little supplemental water, but it performs poorly in heavy, wet, or poorly drained soils, particularly during winter dormancy. Best suited to Mediterranean-climate and warm-temperate gardens in zones 8-10, where it can be sited in a xeric border or rock garden alongside other dry-summer shrubs.

common_name: Spring Fleecing Fringe Tree (Compact Male-Flowering Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Spring Fleecing is a compact, floriferous male native fringe tree selection that sets no fruit.

directions: Spring Fleecing is a compact, densely branched male selection of the native white fringe tree, bred to stay smaller and bloom more heavily than typical seed-grown specimens while reaching only about 10 to 13 feet tall and wide at maturity. Being male, it never sets the messy blue-black fruit produced by female trees, and it channels that energy instead into an especially profuse spring display of long, drooping, fragrant white flower panicles held above narrow, glossy dark-green leaves. Its smaller stature suits foundation plantings, patios, and smaller residential lots where a full-sized fringe tree would eventually crowd the space. Grow in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and expect slow but steady growth with virtually no pest or disease problems once established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in fertile, moist, well-drained, acidic soil high in organic matter, in partial shade with shelter from wind; beaked stewartia does not tolerate drought and needs consistent soil moisture.

directions: Native to mountain forests of southeastern China, beaked stewartia takes its common name from the narrow, pointed buds and fruit capsules that taper to a distinct beak, a detail that distinguishes it from its better-known Japanese and Korean relatives. Slate-gray, ascending branches typically arise in several stems from the base, and from late spring into summer the tree bears the classic stewartia flower: white, cup-shaped, camellia-like blooms with a boss of golden stamens, sometimes lightly flushed pink. Grow in fertile, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade sheltered from strong wind, since this species does not tolerate drought or exposed sites. Its narrower, more upright habit than many garden stewartias makes it a useful specimen for smaller woodland gardens where space is limited.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plant Toolbox
